extracted.intended_audience: NIH grant applicants and PIs preparing Specific Aims pages (R01/K99 and similar)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, tactical guidance for drafting the one-page Specific Aims section of NIH grant applications (R01, K99, etc.), emphasizing structure, voice, preliminary data, and review-readiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read funded Specific Aims in your area first
rubrics_metrics.description: Build a corpus of 10+ funded examples and pattern-match successful structures to learn how funded Aims open, sequence aim 1, and close.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use NIH RePORTER for titles and NIAID or other repositories for full applications; note how funded Aims hook reviewers, what their Aim 1 is, and how they frame impact and feasibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterate the Aims 20+ times
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat the first draft as exploration; iterate many times with staged feedback to tighten and clarify.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Get focused feedback around draft 5, 10, 15 and perform final polish at draft 20+; each iteration should tighten language, clarify claims, and remove hedging.

rubrics_metrics.name: First sentence is make-or-break
rubrics_metrics.description: The opening sentence forms a reviewer impression in seconds and should foreground the problem rather than literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open with concrete information (e.g., prevalence, mortality, market size); avoid abstract framing — concrete > abstract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bold the aims themselves
rubrics_metrics.description: Make aim titles bold and standalone so reviewers can grasp the project from the bold text alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use an aim format like 'Aim 1: [Active verb + key concept]'; the bolded aim title should summarize the aim's action and focus without reading the paragraph.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four-paragraph Specific Aims structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize the page into four clear paragraphs to convey problem, need, approach, and aims/impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paragraph 1 Hook: problem + state of knowledge + critical gap; Paragraph 2 Need: long-term goal + objective + central hypothesis + rationale; Paragraph 3 Approach: strategy + qualifications + innovation; Paragraph 4 Aims: 2–3 numbered aims + closing impact statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim independence doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: Craft aims so each will succeed independently rather than as a serial chain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer parallel logic (three independent threads) so that 'If Aim 1 fails, Aim 2/3 still works'—avoid aims that depend sequentially on previous aims' success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods tax for each aim
rubrics_metrics.description: For every aim include a concise methods-related mini-package that convinces reviewers the aim is feasible and informative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a hypothesis statement, a short approach summary, expected outcomes, and pitfalls & alternatives (these may be explicit or implicit).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use active, declarative voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Write claims and plans in active, direct language (e.g., 'We will determine X').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid passive constructions and weak verbs like 'we hope to' or 'it is anticipated that'; prefer clear declarative sentences that state what will be done or tested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use first-person plural ('we')
rubrics_metrics.description: Even a single PI should use 'we' to signal a team and anchor preliminary data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phrases like 'We have demonstrated' present ownership of preliminary results and project capacity better than passive voice or 'I'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cut hedging ruthlessly
rubrics_metrics.description: Remove weakening words that suggest uncertainty in the main claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid 'could', 'might', 'potentially', 'perhaps' in the main narrative; reserve explicit acknowledgements of uncertainty for the Pitfalls & Alternatives section.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame innovation as a novel application
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer framing innovation as applying established methods to a novel question rather than claiming radical novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers reward feasibility-anchored innovation; cite the methods you adapt. Pure novelty without precedent can trigger skepticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid absolute 'first-ever' claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid unqualified assertions that something is the 'first-ever'—they are often wrong or contested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Safer phrasings include 'To our knowledge, this is the first...' or 'This builds on [prior work] but extends to...'.

rubrics_metrics.name: "So what?" significance test
rubrics_metrics.description: Every paragraph should answer why the work matters—connect the aims to meaningful impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly link to public health, scientific paradigm shifts, or other high-level impacts; do not assume the reviewer already shares your enthusiasm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance is not just citation count
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrate significance through the impact of the proposed work rather than a long list of citations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite key framing papers but avoid exhaustive literature lists; emphasize how YOUR proposed work will move the field or improve health outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary data: quantitative over qualitative
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide quantitative preliminary data with appropriate statistics to support feasibility and effect sizes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include effect sizes, error bars, sample sizes (N), p-values where appropriate, box plots with individual points, replication evidence (e.g., N=3+ biological replicates), and power calculations tied to observed preliminary effect sizes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show your best figure on the Aims page
rubrics_metrics.description: Use one high-impact figure (conceptual or preliminary data) on the Aims page to summarize the project or show compelling data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strong caption should tell the story; the figure should visually support feasibility/impact and is often judged heavily by reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common correlates for single-submission R01 success
rubrics_metrics.description: Patterns observed in threads claiming 'I got my R01 in 1 submission'—factors that frequently appear in those success stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical factors include a senior mentor at a top institution, multiple internal mock reviews, very large numbers of aim iterations (30+), program officer engagement early, and strong preliminary data published in major journals. These are correlates, not guarantees.

rubrics_metrics.name: K99-specific independence and career-development framing
rubrics_metrics.description: For K99 applications, foreground an independence narrative and a concrete career-development plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assemble a mentor team that visibly fills gaps, include named career-development activities, ensure the project is distinct from the sponsor/mentor's portfolio, and include a specific institutional commitment letter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design for reviewer triage and fatigue
rubrics_metrics.description: Format and content choices should account for tired, skeptical reviewers who often treat the Specific Aims page as the whole grant during triage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use bolding/underlining to aid skimming, avoid giving reviewers easy 'nits' to pick on, explicitly address rigor and reproducibility, and make the aims page stand-alone and scannable.
